claims.text: In non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi thin films and nanoribbons, low-field magnetocaloric response and hysteresis are governed by interfacial strain and microstructural defects through their effects on magnetic domain-wall dynamics.
Post-deposition mild annealing partially relieves interfacial stress and reduces defect density.
Annealing-induced stress and defect reduction will lower magnetic hysteresis.
Annealing will produce a more symmetric magnetocaloric temperature-change peak.
As-deposited FeMnNiGeSi nanoscale films and nanoribbons have high densities of defects, grain boundaries, and residual interfacial stresses.
A mild annealing treatment can relieve internal stresses without significant grain coarsening or phase segregation.
Heat-transfer rate limits the usable frequency of the magnetic-cooling cycles.
Keeping film thickness and lateral dimensions nanoscale preserves low-dimensionality effects.
Interfacial strains, grain boundaries, and dislocations act as pinning centers for magnetic domain walls.
Magnetoelastic coupling in FeMnNiGeSi causes local interfacial strain fields to pin magnetic domain walls during field cycling.
Annealing reduces local stresses and defect concentrations, thereby decreasing the energy barriers for domain-wall reversal.
Reduced domain pinning leads to lower coercivity and hysteresis loss.
Reduced domain-wall pinning produces a more reversible magnetocaloric effect.
Annealed samples will have narrower magnetic hysteresis loops than as-deposited samples.
Annealing may slightly shift the peak magnetocaloric temperature by altering domain-reconfiguration dynamics.
The as-deposited baseline has higher hysteresis and a more asymmetric magnetocaloric temperature-change response because of abundant defects and stress-induced domain-wall pinning.
The proposed mechanism operates at applied fields from tens to a few hundred oersted and near the FeMnNiGeSi magnetocaloric transition.
At sufficiently high cycle frequency, heat-transfer limitations can dominate and substantially change the observed response.
